question: A learning specialist is configuring a Project for course-design work. Their organization has an internal instructional-design standard and a preferred output structure for lesson outlines. Which custom-instruction set best supports this use case? A. Name Claude’s role as a course designer; let each chat’s prompt specify the standards and output structure for that lesson, since lessons vary widely. B. Name Claude’s role as a course designer and require alignment to the organization’s instructional-design standards; leave output structure to Claude based on the topic of each lesson. C. Specify only the preferred output structure for lesson outlines, since the structure carries the standards implicitly and naming the role adds no value. D. Name Claude’s role as a course designer, require alignment to the organization’s instructional-design standards, and specify the preferred output structure for lesson outlines.

Preparing an AI-assisted work product for external delivery, a senior manager is applying the AI Fluency Framework Diligence competency. Which step best reflects Diligence principles? A. Deliver the work product without independent verification on the basis that AI assistance shifts accountability away from the human, even though Diligence holds the human fully accountable for the output. B. Delegate accountability for the AI-assisted work product to Claude itself rather than retaining it as a human obligation, contrary to the Diligence principle that humans remain accountable for AI-assisted outputs. C. Skip verification of any element on the assumption that fluent output implies accuracy, even though Diligence requires the human to verify and correct AI-assisted outputs before they are acted upon. D. Identify the elements of the work product that must be independently verified or corrected before delivery, and take ownership of those verifications as a professional accountability obligation.

You are a customer-success lead running an interactive workflow where each turn must respond quickly and the per-turn reasoning is light. Which selection best aligns to the requirements? A. Choose any model because latency does not vary by model. B. Choose Haiku to keep latency low and to handle a light reasoning load efficiently at scale. C. Choose Opus to maximize reasoning depth despite higher latency. D. Choose a model based on the alphabetical order of its name.

You are a Claude associate assessing a proposed Claude use case before approving it for your team. Which is the correct order of assessment steps? (1) Compare the use case against the organization’s policies and the relevant regulatory considerations. (2) Document the assessment outcome and the rationale for traceability. (3) Identify the audience, decision impact, and reversibility of the outputs. (4) Decide whether the use case proceeds, requires modification, or is declined. (5) Identify the data types involved and whether sensitive data is implicated. A. 3, 1, 5, 4, 2 B. 1, 3, 5, 4, 2 C. 5, 3, 1, 4, 2 D. 3, 5, 1, 4, 2

You are a knowledge worker deciding whether to escalate a Claude-generated output. Which is the correct order of decision steps? (1) Identify the audience and the impact of the output if it is wrong. (2) Document the decision and the rationale for traceability. (3) Compare the output’s risk profile to the organization’s escalation criteria. (4) Decide whether to use, iterate further, or escalate. (5) Assess the output’s accuracy, completeness, and any unverified claims. A. 5, 1, 3, 4, 2 B. 3, 1, 5, 4, 2 C. 1, 5, 3, 4, 2 D. 1, 3, 5, 4, 2

A Claude associate is identifying the bottleneck in a content workflow that takes too long to publish. The workflow has five steps: research, drafting, internal review, legal review, and publication. There is cycle-time data for each step from the past month. Which signal most directly identifies the bottleneck? A. the step where individual contributors report the highest workload based on their weekly status updates B. the step most recently added to the workflow, based on the assumption that process changes introduce the most friction C. the step with the longest queue or the largest backlog of items waiting to enter it D. the step with the highest average cycle time per item across the past month’s runs

You are a Claude associate troubleshooting a recurring poor output. Which is the correct order of diagnostic steps? (1) Form a hypothesis about which prompt element most likely caused the deficiency. (2) Apply a single targeted change and observe the effect on the output. (3) Read the output end to end and identify the specific deficiency. (4) Compare the deficient output to the prompt to spot mismatches between input and output. (5) Document the root cause and the resolution for future reference. A. 1, 3, 4, 2, 5 B. 4, 3, 1, 2, 5 C. 3, 1, 4, 2, 5 D. 3, 4, 1, 2, 5

You are reviewing claims about prompt iteration that colleagues have made in a recent training. Which two claims about prompt iteration are accurate? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution. A. Repeated resubmission of the same prompt is the most reliable way to improve output. B. Output comparison against original criteria validates whether iteration helped. C. Iteration is most productive when each change targets a specific diagnosed weakness. D. Iteration should stop only after every possible alternative phrasing has been tried. E. More iterations always produce a better output regardless of what was changed.

A Claude associate is reviewing a Claude-drafted set of customer-segment descriptions for an internal marketing brief. One description applies a generalization about a demographic group’s purchasing behavior that does not hold for individual customers in the segment. Which response is most appropriate? A. Revise the description to focus on observed behaviors rather than generalizations about people, and validate the revision against actual customer data. B. Remove the entire customer-segment description from the brief, since any segmentation that involves demographic characteristics is likely to introduce similar issues. C. Keep the description as written for the internal brief, since internal use does not carry the same risk as external publication of demographic generalizations. D. Add a disclaimer to the description, noting that the generalization may not apply to all individuals in the segment, and keep the underlying description unchanged.

As part of a workflow redesign, a process analyst is applying the AI Fluency Framework Delegation competency. Which two criteria most directly inform Delegation decisions? (Choose two.) A. The reversibility of the task and the consequence of an error, which together indicate whether the step is safe to delegate to Claude or should be retained for human decision-making. B. The need for human creativity, empathy, or judgment in the step, which indicates whether the task is appropriate for AI delegation or requires the human capabilities Claude cannot provide. C. The visual complexity of the workflow diagram, since steps with more connections and dependencies are more likely to require human oversight. D. The seniority of the team member who currently performs the step, since more senior roles typically involve higher-stakes tasks that warrant human retention. E. The length of time the workflow has existed in its current form, since well-established processes have been sufficiently validated for AI delegation.

A Claude associate is evaluating whether to enable a Skill that was provided by an unfamiliar third party. Which two checks best support a sound trust decision? (Choose two.) A. Verify the source of the Skill against the organization’s approved-Skill list before enabling it within claude.ai or any Project the team uses for its work. B. Treat the Skill's appearance in a public listing as sufficient validation, without confirming the source, the requested permissions, or alignment with the organization’s approved-Skill list. C. Skip permission review on the assumption that the Skill cannot exceed the boundaries of the workflow, even though Skills can request access that the task does not require. D. Review the permissions and capabilities the Skill requests and confirm that the requested access is appropriate for the task the Skill is intended to perform. E. Enable the Skill immediately on the basis of strong external reviews, even though the source has not been validated against the organization’s approved-Skill list and the permissions remain unverified.

You are a project lead reviewing a teammate’s habit of using the same prompt template for every task regardless of type. Which feedback is most warranted? A. The prompting strategy should be adapted to each task type because one template does not produce equally strong outputs across all tasks. B. The habit is ideal because a single template guarantees consistent quality across all task types. C. The prompting strategy should not change between tasks because adapting it wastes time and adds no value. D. Task type has no effect on the appropriate prompting strategy.

You are a knowledge worker summarizing common prompt failure patterns for the team. Which pattern most often produces vague or off-target output? A. a prompt that names a topic but does not state the task, audience, or required output structure B. a prompt that adds clear constraints on length and tone C. a prompt that explicitly names the role, task, audience, and required output format D. a prompt that includes a representative example of the desired output

A finance manager must select a Claude feature for a task that requires deterministic calculations across a multi-tab spreadsheet. Which selection best fits the requirement? A. Use an Artifact alone for the calculations, which provides a stable editable surface for the result but does not perform the deterministic computation that Code Execution would run. B. Use Code Execution, which runs code in a sandbox to perform calculations on the uploaded file and produce verified outputs the associate can check. C. Use the Research feature for the calculations, which gathers and synthesizes external sources and is not the appropriate feature for deterministic computation on an uploaded spreadsheet. D. Use a standard chat prompt for the calculations, which generates text without running code and does not produce the verified deterministic output the multi-tab calculation task requires.

You are a senior analyst using Claude to analyze requirements from several stakeholder sources. Which is the correct order of steps? (1) Group related requirements and flag conflicts or ambiguities for stakeholder review. (2) Validate the structured output against the original sources for accuracy and completeness. (3) Submit the consolidated inputs to Claude with a structured extraction prompt. (4) Gather and label the source materials so each requirement can be traced. (5) Document the final requirements set with source traceability and status. A. 4, 1, 3, 2, 5 B. 4, 3, 1, 2, 5 C. 1, 4, 3, 2, 5 D. 3, 4, 1, 2, 5

You are organizing connected data sources for a team and must complete the planning steps before authorizing any connection. Which two planning steps must be completed BEFORE authorizing a new Connector? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution. A. Migrate every existing report off the prior data source onto the new Connector. B. Confirm the Connector is on the approved-vendor list maintained by IT. C. Confirm the data classification of the source and the team’s permission to use it. D. Train every team member on the new Connector through formal training sessions. E. Decommission any unused legacy connectors that may still be authorized.

You are a business analyst evaluating a Claude-generated business case against the agreed acceptance criteria. Which is the correct order of evaluation steps? (1) Compare the business case to the source data and required topics. (2) Document gaps and inaccuracies for follow-up or correction. (3) Restate the acceptance criteria for the business case. (4) Decide whether to use the business case, iterate, or escalate. (5) Read the business case end to end to form an initial impression. A. 3, 1, 5, 2, 4 B. 1, 3, 5, 2, 4 C. 5, 3, 1, 2, 4 D. 3, 5, 1, 2, 4
